why: Every first-party service the real handler reaches is an object literal; the scenario proves the stubs.

excerpt:
Given('a hotel with one free double room')(() => Effect.void),
When('the guest reserves it')('booked', () => handlers.handle('reserve_room', input).pipe(Effect.provide(oneFreeRoomHeld))),
why: The Given builds nothing; the state it claims is smuggled in through a stub layer the When provides.

excerpt:
Feature('a guest reserves a room')
  .live('the handler needs the real clock')
  .withScenarioLayer(Layer.empty)
why: A .live reason string does not supply a world; the Givens claim stored state and the scenario layer is empty.

excerpt:
Given('every HOTEL_ variable set, with 20 rooms')(() => Effect.void),
When('the reservation service reads its settings')('config', () => hotelConfig.pipe(Effect.provide(ConfigProvider.layer(ConfigProvider.fromUnknown(settings))))),
why: Decodes a config layer directly under a provider the When builds; a unit test of configuration, which gets no test.

excerpt:
Feature('the price list is built from the rate files').withScenarioLayer(Layer.empty)
  Given('a deluxe room rated at 120 a night')(() => Effect.void),
  When('the price list is built')('prices', () => Effect.sync(() => priceListOf({ rates: literalFiles }))),
why: An internal pure function fed literal fixtures in an empty world, under a Feature title.

excerpt: When('the guest asks for rates')('answer', () => quote(['deluxe']).pipe(Effect.provide(quoteHandlers.pipe(Layer.provideMerge(Layer.succeed(RateCard, RateCard.of({ rates }))))))),
why: The port the handler reads is hand-built inline with no contract suite; the answer is whatever the stub returns.

excerpt: Then('the guest was emailed once')(({ held }, expect) => expect(held.sent).toEqual(['confirmation'])),
why: The record is kept by an inline stub that no contract suite runs, so what it says the system sent proves nothing. A contract-suite fake's read operation would pass (see gold-outbound-port-read-back).

excerpt: And('the room row is marked reserved')(({ db, room }, expect) => Effect.flatMap(readRoomRow(db, room.id), (row) => expect(row).toMatchObject({ state: 'reserved' }))),
why: The verdict is for this step, not the scenario: it queries the table, an outcome buried inside the system. The step is rewritten to read the outcome through the system's own operations (Gherkin's reference: resist looking in the database), and the rest of the scenario stands.

excerpt:
Given('rates/deluxe.json holds nightly: 120 under the standard season key')(() => writeFixture(files)),
When('priceListOf runs over the rate map')('prices', () => buildPrices(files)),
why: The wording names a file layout and an internal function; it would change with the implementation.

excerpt:
.withScenarioLayer(testLayer) // real services over the test store; only the payment provider is a fake
Given('a hotel with one free double room')('room', ({ rooms }) => rooms.add({ kind: 'double' })),
When('Grace reserves a double room')('result', ({ reservations }) => reservations.execute(new Reserve({ guest: GRACE, kind: 'double' }))),
Then('Grace gets the last double room')(({ result }, expect) => expect(result).toMatchObject({ status: 'confirmed', remaining: 0 })),
why: Given puts the room in place, When is the guest's command through the service's entry, and one Then reads only what that command returns, with the expect the step receives.

excerpt:
Given('a hotel with one free double room')(({ rooms }) => rooms.add({ kind: 'double' })),
When('Grace and Henry reserve it at the same moment')('results', ({ reservations }) => Effect.all([reserve(GRACE), reserve(HENRY)], { concurrency: 2 })),
Then('exactly one of them gets the room')(({ results }, expect) => expect(results.map(Either.isRight).sort()).toEqual([false, true])),
why: A race specified as behaviour against the real store through the consumer's entry.

excerpt:
background(emptyTheHotel)
scenario('a guest is turned away when nothing is free', scope.pipe(
  When('Grace reserves a double room')('result', ({ reservations }) => reservations.execute(new Reserve({ guest: GRACE, kind: 'double' })).pipe(Effect.either)),
  Then('she is told no rooms are free')(({ result }, expect) => expect(result).toMatchObject(Either.left({ _tag: 'NoRoomsFree' }))),
why: Edge case: no Given is needed because the background really empties the store; the empty state is true, not claimed.
The only fake is a third-party port, built as a service with failure controls and read-back operations and run in its contract suite; every first-party service runs its real layer.

Edge case: supplying the settings service with values is how tests provide settings (configuration pack), not a stubbed first-party service; question 4 passes. The scenario specifies the consumer's refusal, not the setting.
Question 3 allows what our system sent through its own outbound port, read in the port's terms through a contract-suite fake's read operation.
